newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK activist drowns protesting Japan claim to isles.
newsitem.headline: HK activist drowns protesting Japan claim to isles.

text.p: A Hong Kong activist leapt to his death in a roiling East China Sea on Thursday after Japanese patrol boats thwarted his protest ship's bid to land on a disputed archipelago to claim it back for China.
David Chan, 45, and four other protesters had jumped into the storm-whipped sea, vowing to defy even Japan's claim to waters surrounding the uninhabited cluster of islands.

Chan's death was the first in a wave of protests to sweep Hong Kong, Taiwan, Macau and China since July, when Japanese ultranationalists built a lighthouse and raised Japan's flag on the islands northeast of Taiwan to assert Tokyo's sovereignty.

The tragedy aboard the rusty tanker Kien Hwa 2, witnessed by reporters aboard the nearby fishing boat Hanghai, brought expressions of regret in Hong Kong, Tokyo, Beijing and Taipei -- and calls for cooler heads.
But it also heightened tension between Japan, which has claimed the islands since 1895 as the Senkakus, and China, which calls them the Diaoyus and has claimed them for centuries.

China, keen to marshal patriotism stirred by the sovereignty row without offending Japanese investors, reiterated its call for Tokyo to restrain right-wing activists whose actions have whipped up Chinese nationalism against Japan.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said China had an "unshakeable" will to safeguard its territory and urged Japan to act to prevent a further deterioration of the dispute.
Japan, which has sought to cool Chinese anger, issued a statement citing the "utmost efforts" of Japanese medics to save Chan and regretting his death "from the heart".
"We strongly hope this type of incident is never repeated," Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto said.
Early on Friday, the Kien Hwa and its sombre passengers put into port in Taiwan's Keelung for the grim task of returning Chan's body to Hong Kong.
The ship complied with Taiwan's request not to fly rival China's red flag as it came into port at Keelung, nor was it used to wrap Chan's body as it was put ashore.
"I couldn't grasp what was going through my mind," Hong Kong reporter Jackson Liao recalled as he stepped from the Kien Hwa. "I saw this man die right by my feet."
"Down with Japanese imperialism!" some 200 sympathetic Taiwan protesters chanted at Keelung. "Protect the Diaoyus!"
Fearing a nationalist backlash, Japan's Hong Kong diplomatic mission sought police protection for all Japanese organisations in the British territory, including private firms.
The ship had set out from Hong Kong on Sunday, with protest leader Chan vowing to plant China's flag on the islands and pull down Japan's flag and the offending lighthouse.
Some 17 Japanese coastal patrol boats and several aircraft circled the tanker as it neared the islands, allowing it no closer than two nautical miles offshore early on Thursday.
It was after the ship's pilot opposed a proposed landing by rubber raft that Chan and four others donned life vests, tied themselves to ropes and dived into the sea.
Chan, a non-swimmer, lost consciousness as he was dragged beside the ship for 15 minutes, often below the heavy waves.
Protesters initially seemed not to sense the seriousness of Chan's plight. Though alive when pulled aboard, he could not be revived by crew or Japanese medics put aboard by helicopter.
A Japanese doctor declared Chan dead.
Another protester was seriously injured and flown to Okinawa in southern Japan. Three were plucked from the sea unhurt.
Grief swept those aboard the Kien Hwa 2. "When it happened everybody felt very saddened," activist Ma Ding said in Taiwan.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule in mid-1997 and many Hong Kong people see the dispute as a test of China's strength and integrity.
